source.title: The Knowledge Microscope: Features as Better Analytical Lenses than Neurons
source.authors: Yuheng Chen; Pengfei Cao; Kang Liu; Jun Zhao

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines SAE-derived features in Gemma-2 language models and factual-knowledge tasks, extending feature-based evidence to LLMs. It does not reproduce the original toy-network experiments or measure their feature geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper cites toy-model superposition and discusses it as background, but reports no toy-network experiment, feature-angle or overlap-geometry measurement, sparsity sweep, or test of capacity competition. Its own relevant results concern SAE features in Gemma-2 factual-knowledge tasks and their stability across SAE feature-count settings. FeatureEdit privacy-erasure results are omitted because they report the performance of the study's new downstream method, not a test of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study runs Gemma Scope SAEs on Gemma-2 2B/9B factual recall and compares SAE features with neurons and with PCA, ICA and random bases. It reports ablation impact, interpretability and fact-specific activation separation. These results bear on V4: an SAE recovers sparse, more monosemantic units than neurons in a real LM. There are no toy-model, capacity or multi-dimensional-feature experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAE features beat neurons as units for factual knowledge in Gemma-2: more impact on knowledge expression, better interpretability and stronger monosemanticity, with FeatureEdit better at privacy erasure. On feature-count settings, they claim stability across N but explicitly leave open whether the feature space is truly insensitive to N.
record.recipe_differences: The original work studies superposition in toy networks; this paper uses pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs and factual-knowledge datasets to compare features and neurons in Gemma-2 LMs. It does not reproduce the original toy-network method or geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different outcomes by transformer component, model size, relation-fact proportion, and SAE feature-count multiplier N. Its monosemanticity analysis varies relation-fact proportion from 0% to 100% in 20% increments; its feature-localization analysis varies n from 1 to 8.
record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and dataset will be available
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Evidence is limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B and factual-knowledge experiments. Some relevant results are presented only in figures in the supplied text. The feature-count stability test concerns localization overlap across N, not completeness, canonicality, or stability across independently trained dictionaries.
record.rows_left_out: FeatureEdit privacy-erasure results in §5 and Figure 9 were left out because they evaluate the study's downstream editing method rather than the claim versions' representation or geometry. The paper's cited toy-model findings are prior work, not results of this study.

untested.parts: No toy models, geometry, near-orthogonality or sparsity transition.
Capacity competition is only asserted (facts outnumber neurons), not tested.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Whether individual features are spread across many neurons is not directly measured. Only Gemma-2 2B/9B on factual recall.
Completeness, canonicality and seed stability are untested. The cross-N stability measure cannot establish feature identity.

missing.what: Neuron-side monosemanticity results: neurons active at 0% relation-facts, and Table 5 neuron effect sizes (2B 80 vs 60 d = −0.13; 9B 80 vs 60 d = 0.41).
Single-unit results: ablating one post-MLP feature gives ΔProb ≈0.6, about 3× a neuron. Per-unit IS is ≈0.7 for top features versus <0.4 for neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The V5 support label was dropped: the overlap metric relies on index correspondence between SAEs of different widths, which the method does not justify. The IS comparison uses gpt-4o-mini predictions on only 6 samples per unit. The 2B SAE vs ICA ΔProb advantage is small (d = 0.38). FeatureEdit results were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test toy models, sparse-feature overlap geometry, near-orthogonality, or a sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry.
The paper asserts that factual items may outnumber neurons, but does not test whether capacity pressure causes important features to receive dedicated dimensions while others share.

The paper measures activation differences between features and neurons but does not test whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure or whether it is evidence for superposition.
The study tests SAE-derived features in Gemma-2 factual-knowledge tasks. It does not measure whether features are spread across many neurons, or establish this for models beyond Gemma-2.

It tests feature-localization consistency across feature-count multipliers, but not whether SAE features are complete or canonical, or whether they are stable across SAE training seeds, dictionaries, or other settings.
The paper uses scalar SAE feature activations but does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Ablate SAE-derived features and measure the change in correct-answer probability; compare feature-acquisition methods.
rows.baseline: PCA, ICA and random-direction comparisons; exact baseline value not stated
rows.note: The authors report that SAE features perform better than the compared methods in both models, but the extracted figure text does not provide a reliably assignable Gemma-2 2B value.
rows.check: The value is readable from the Figure 2 labels: Gemma-2 2B SAE ΔProb ≈0.73, versus roughly 0.58/0.52/0.05 for the other methods. Table 2 gives SAE vs ICA Cohen's d = 0.38, a small effect. The baseline should cite Table 2 effect sizes rather than 'not stated'.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compare feature-localization positions at multiplier n with the expected positions based on n=1; report average overlap ratio.
rows.note: The authors interpret the high overlap as consistency in feature localization across feature counts.
rows.check: Overlap compares feature index positions at n>1 with the expected range [position×n, (position+1)×n−1]. Indices in separately trained SAEs carry no correspondence, so overlap of index positions cannot show that the same features recur across dictionary sizes. Appendix D.5 also describes a different (sigmoid) SAE from the JumpReLU Gemma Scope SAEs, so it is unclear which dictionaries were compared.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2 2B and 9B, Gemma Scope SAEs, ParaRel factual recall
relationships.reason: SAE features beat PCA, ICA and random bases (R01–R04) and beat neurons on IS (R07–R08). Features activate fact-specifically while neurons fire at 0% relevant input (R09–R12), so the SAE recovers sparse, more monosemantic units.
relationships.display_finding: SAE features beat PCA, ICA and random bases and outperformed neurons on IS. Features activated fact-specifically while neurons fired on 0% relevant input, so the SAE units were sparser and more monosemantic.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports SAE-derived features with stronger ablation impact and interpretability than comparison methods or neurons, and feature activation patterns that vary with relation-fact proportion (R01-R12).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Feature-localization overlap across n=1, 2, 4 and 8 in Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 2 9B
reader_labels.reason: Reported average overlap ratios are high across the tested feature-count multipliers, including values above 0.87 at n=8; this supports consistency across this particular setting, not completeness or canonicality (R13-R18).
